meta.title: Who really said "He who has injured thee was either stronger or weaker than thee. If weaker, spare him; if stronger, spare thyself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No, Shakespeare never wrote this. It is Seneca the Younger, from On Anger (De Ira), Book III, ch. 5 — the Stoic counsel to spare the weak and spare yourself.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who has injured thee was either stronger or weaker than thee. If weaker, spare him; if stronger, spare thyself'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare — it's Seneca the Younger, from On Anger (De Ira), Book III. An older translation of the Stoic line on responding to injury.

answer.label: Not William Shakespeare — actually Seneca the Younger
answer.authorDates: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher & statesman
answer.sourceLine: This is not Shakespeare. It comes from the Roman Stoic Seneca the Younger, in his essay On Anger (De Ira), Book III, ch. 5, where he argues that revenge only admits you were wounded. The much-shared “thee … thyself” wording is an older English rendering of Seneca’s Latin; the standard scholarly translation by Aubrey Stewart (1900) reads “He who has hurt you must be either stronger or weaker than yourself. If he be weaker, spare him: if he be stronger, spare yourself ↗.”

source.excerpt: “He who has hurt you must be either stronger or weaker than yourself. If he be weaker, spare him: if he be stronger, spare yourself.”
trail: The line is Stoic counsel from Seneca’s On Anger, Book III, ch. 5 ↗, not anything Shakespeare wrote.
Quotation references credit it to Seneca — WIST cites Moral Essays, “On Anger” ↗ and Libquotes cites De Ira ↗.
The Shakespeare tag is a common web error, e.g. Quotefancy prints it under Shakespeare’s name ↗.
source.excerptNote: Aubrey Stewart’s 1900 translation of the passage. The circulating “He who has injured thee … spare thyself” version is an older English rendering of the same Latin sentence (“si inbecillior, parce illi, si potentior, tibi”).

source.rightsNote: Seneca’s Latin De Ira (1st century AD) is long in the public domain, and the archaic “thee/thyself” English wording is an old (pre-1931) translation. The standard scholarly English translation quoted here, Aubrey Stewart’s 1900 version, is also public domain in the United States.

author.heading: About Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman & dramatist
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (Seneca the Younger) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and tragedian who served as tutor and adviser to the emperor Nero. His moral essays and Letters to Lucilius are cornerstones of practical Stoicism. De Ira (“On Anger”), the three-book dialogue this line comes from, is his sustained argument that anger is a destructive and avoidable passion.

misattribution.heading: How Shakespeare got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine Seneca line that has drifted onto Shakespeare’s name on quote sites and social media — a classic case of a wise-sounding aphorism migrating to the most famous name available.

items.why: Numerous quote aggregators file the line under Shakespeare with no play, sonnet or line reference — e.g. Quotefancy ↗ and Quotes.net ↗. It appears in none of Shakespeare’s works; the archaic “thee/thyself” diction is from a translation of Latin, not Elizabethan English verse.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Seneca’s, from On Anger (De Ira), Book III, ch. 5 ↗ — a Stoic argument against revenge, rendered into older English and later mis-tagged to Shakespeare.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In On Anger, Seneca urges that retaliation is beneath a person of real magnitude: to avenge an insult is to concede you were hurt by it. The line sits inside his larger case that anger is a voluntary, ruinous passion best refused outright.
The logic is deliberately tidy: whoever wronged you was either weaker or stronger; the weak deserve mercy, and against the strong, restraint spares you the greater damage of escalation.
